awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Proposal: MRA: The influence of climatic dipoles on plant and animal populations at continental scales
awd_abstract_narration:
Changes in climate often result in the appearance of unusually warm and dry conditions in one part of the world with cold and wet conditions thousands of miles away. These lasting and predictable fluctuations in temperature and rainfall are known as "climatic dipoles" and often emerge across years or decades. A well-known example of this phenomenon is El Nino, where wet conditions across the southern United States are associated with dry conditions to the north. Most ecological studies collect data at local or regional scales. As a result, the continental-scale effects of climatic dipoles on ecological and environmental processes are largely unexplored. Climatic dipoles may provide insight on important phenomena such as animal migrations, agricultural and forest productivity, insect outbreaks, and the emergence of diseases. This study will use long-term observations of bird movements from thousands of citizen scientists, decades of seed production records in trees, and animal population numbers collected throughout the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON). The project will partner with and guide existing citizen science programs to better predict the effects of climate on animals and plants. The team will organize "ecoclimatology" workshops to provide training to early-career scientists interested in both climate science as well as ecology.

The research poses a novel framework of methods applied for space-time pattern discovery, used by climate scientists to analyze variability, to identify climate-ecological dipoles across North America. The overarching hypothesis is that many ecological phenomena are entrained at continental scales by dipole modes of climate variability. Specific questions include: 1) do atmospheric circulations and climatic dipoles synchronize seed production in trees (known as masting) and avian irruptions at continental scales?; 2) do unique modes of climate variability affect the population dynamics for multiple taxa (seed-dependent birds, small mammals, and ticks) at disjunct NEON sites and across multiple time lags?; and 3) how might historic and future environmental change influence these climatic-ecological relationships? Analyzing three decades of data from Project FeederWatch and a recently compiled data set of tree masting at hundreds of sites, the research will explore the use of empirical orthogonal functions to understand climate variability impacting plant and animal communities during a time of rapid environmental change. Ecological observatory networks, such as NEON, and citizen science databases are increasingly rich in information. Employing these analytical approaches from climate science will represent a key advance for ecological research.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Our project brought together research at the intersection of climate science, ecology, and ecosystem processes to explore how climate patterns called "climatic dipoles" influence plant and animal populations across North America. By combining studies on climate patterns and ecological responses, we uncovered new insights into how changes in climate ripple through natural systems, affecting both wildlife and plant relationships across continents.

Changes in climate do not happen evenly across the planet. Often, when one region experiences unusually hot and dry conditions, another area thousands of kilometers away, experiences cooler and wetter weather. These long-lasting, predictable patterns are known by climatologists as “climatic dipoles”. Conversely, ecological research has historically investigated changes in local environments that are relatively close together and how it affects populations of plants and animals. Much less has been known about how climate dipoles affect ecosystems across entire continents. Understanding these linkages sheds light on some impressive events in nature, including winter bird migrations outside of the normal range of some species, patterns of immense seed production by trees, and insect outbreaks. Our project tackled that challenge by combining decades of ecological and climate data at sites spanning distances across  North America. We relied on bird observations collected by thousands of citizen scientists, long-term records of tree seed production, and animal population data from the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON). By bringing these datasets together, scientists were able to address questions that were not possible before.

A key finding  was the discovery of a climate-masting-irruption dipole across North America. This means that large-scale climate conditions, such as fluctuations in temperature, synchronized ecological events across vast areas. For example, in North America, climate shifts can drive years of unusually high seed production (masting) by trees, which in turn lead to population booms and widespread movements (irruptions) of wildlife such as birds and mammals. These findings demonstrate that ecological events we often think of as local are, in fact, linked to continental and even global climate drivers. As climate change continues, the timing and strength of these links are expected to shift, reshaping ecosystems and species interactions.

Another key result came from research into the North American Dipole, a summer climate pattern that produces hot, dry conditions in some regions and cooler, wetter conditions in others. By examining what drives this dipole, we improved our understanding of the processes behind droughts, heat waves, and floods. Because these patterns strongly affect agriculture and water resources, this work could contribute to better seasonal forecasting and can help communities prepare for climate extremes before they occur.

By linking large-scale climate patterns to wildlife movements and seed production, we bridged climatology and ecology in ways that had not been attempted before. Studies of the North American Dipole revealed why and how regional extremes develop, providing building blocks for better climate models. Together, these outcomes enrich our scientific knowledge of climate–ecosystem interactions across scales, from bird migration to continental weather systems.

Beyond scientific discoveries, this project provided training for four graduate students (2 PhD, 2 MS), a post-BS technician, and multiple undergraduates, emphasizing interdisciplinary research spanning climatology, ecology, and ornithology. Our findings were shared through presentations at major scientific conferences, news articles covering our work, and writing scientific papers. By bridging gaps between ecology and climatology, this research advances our understanding of continent-wide ecological processes and enhances public awareness of the connections between climate and biodiversity.

Ultimately, our work is opening a new window into how ecosystems operate at continental scales. By blending the power of citizen science, long-term ecological networks, and climate research, it offers fresh insights into how our changing climate shapes the natural world we all depend on.
